planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring once soil has warmed; Bruce is one of the named canistel selections long evaluated at Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden's canistel trial and needs frost protection its first winters in zone 9.

directions: Bruce is a Fairchild-evaluated canistel selection known for unusually large fruit, commonly 6-24 ounces, with moist, deep-orange pulp and a heavy, dependable bearing habit compared to seedling trees. Grow in full sun on well-drained, fertile soil and expect several years before a young grafted tree reaches bearing size. The texture is drier than most fruit and strongly custard-like, so Bruce canistel is most often eaten mashed into milkshakes, flans, or baked goods rather than fresh out of hand. Pick fruit when the skin has turned fully yellow-orange and glossy, then hold it at room temperature until it softens completely before eating.
sources: Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden canistel evaluation program
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Canistel Growing in the Home Landscape

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring; Oro is another named canistel selection long evaluated alongside Bruce in South Florida's cottage-industry canistel trials.

directions: Oro canistel bears slightly moist, very sweet flesh with notably good flavor compared to run-of-the-mill seedling trees, and its name (Spanish for gold) nods to the rich orange-gold color of the ripe pulp. Grow it the same way as other grafted canistel selections, in full sun on well-drained soil, with young trees needing winter protection until well established. It flowers and sets fruit over an extended season, giving a longer harvest window than many single-flush tree fruits. Allow fruit to fully soften at room temperature after harvest, since the dense, sweet-potato-like flesh is unpleasantly dry and starchy if eaten underripe.
sources: Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden canistel evaluation program
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Canistel Growing in the Home Landscape

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after frost danger passes, in a warm, sheltered spot; protect young trunks through the first several winters in zone 9b-10.

directions: Excalibur is a named grafted black sapote selection, originating from Excalibur Nursery, grown for reliable fruit set and good eating quality on a glossy-leaved evergreen tree. Like other black sapote cultivars it needs several years after transplanting before it bears, but then crops heavily through fall and winter when little else is fresh on the Gulf Coast. Grow in full sun to light shade on well-drained, fertile soil, and keep young trees watered during dry spells to support steady growth. Harvest fruit while still firm and green, then let it soften fully at room temperature for a week or more before spooning out the dark, pudding-textured flesh.
sources: Rare fruit nursery cultivar notes (Excalibur Nursery)
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Black Sapote in the Home Landscape

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in a warm, sheltered location; Wilson was named for grower Richard Wilson of Excalibur Nursery and needs winter protection while young in zone 9b-10.

directions: Wilson is a named black sapote selection noted for exceptional flavor, with tasters describing notes of cinnamon and allspice in the ripe pulp beyond the usual mild chocolate-pudding character of the species. Grow it like other grafted black sapote on well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light shade, and expect the glossy evergreen tree to need several years to reach bearing size. Fruit ripens over an extended fall-into-winter season and must be picked firm and green, then ripened indoors at room temperature until fully soft. Use the sweet, custardy flesh in smoothies, puddings, and baked goods just as with other black sapote selections.
sources: Rare fruit nursery cultivar notes (Excalibur Nursery)
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Black Sapote in the Home Landscape

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; Lolita is a named selection grown for its large, black-ripening fruit and notably sweet flavor with little of the species' typical resinous aftertaste.

directions: Lolita is a dark-fruited Surinam cherry selection prized for very sweet, juicy fruit that ripens nearly black and lacks the bitter, resinous edge common in seedling-grown red forms. Grow it in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light shade, watering regularly through bloom and fruit set; established plants shrug off brief light frosts and tolerate pruning well enough to be grown as a dense fruiting hedge. Plants flush into fragrant white flowers followed by ribbed, lantern-shaped fruit several times a year in warm climates. Pick fruit only once it has turned fully dark and softened slightly, since underripe fruit of even this sweeter selection is strongly astringent.
sources: Rare Fruit Council International cultivar notes

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring; Choiceana is a California selection (originated by William Boyes of Lomita) that is only partially self-fruitful, so a second cultivar planted nearby meaningfully improves fruit set.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Choiceana is a moderately vigorous, spreading feijoa selection originated in California by grower William Boyes of Lomita, later exported to Australia and New Zealand. Fruit is small to medium, round to oval, with fairly smooth skin and good aromatic, pineapple-guava flavor, ripening in midseason to extend the harvest window when grown alongside earlier or later cultivars. It sets only a partial crop on its own pollen, so interplanting a second, genetically distinct cultivar meaningfully improves yield. Established plants tolerate brief hard freezes well into zone 8, and the showy white-and-crimson spring flowers with sweet, edible petals are a bonus harvest of their own. Let fruit ripen fully and drop naturally rather than picking, since feijoa develops its best flavor only after it falls from the branch.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Feijoa Fruit Facts
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Growing Feijoa Fruit in Florida

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring; Edenvale Supreme was bred by Frank Serpa at Edenvale Nurseries in Santa Cruz, California, and like most feijoa cultivars benefits from a genetically distinct partner planted nearby for best fruit set.

directions: Edenvale Supreme is one of several feijoa selections bred by Frank Serpa at Edenvale Nurseries, producing medium-sized, oblong fruit of very good to excellent flavor and quality that ripens in November, between the earlier Edenvale Improved Coolidge and the later Edenvale Late. Grow in full sun on well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil, and interplant with a second cultivar since Supreme sets fruit poorly on its own pollen alone. Established plants tolerate brief dips into the mid-teens Fahrenheit, making the shrub reliable through zone 8 and 9 on the Gulf Coast. Allow fruit to ripen and fall naturally before gathering it, since feijoa picked too early never develops its full aromatic, pineapple-mint flavor.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Feijoa Fruit Facts
CRFG Fruit Facts: Feijoa cultivar notes

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees well after last frost in a warm, sheltered spot; this species is more cold-sensitive than the common black jaboticaba and is best suited to zone 9b-10 with winter protection while young, or large-container culture further north.

directions: Jaboticaba branca, also called ibatinga, is a Brazilian relative of the familiar black jaboticaba (Plinia cauliflora) that fruits the same way, in dense clusters sprouting directly from the trunk and older branches, but ripens to a pale yellow-green rather than purple-black skin. The thin-skinned fruit has translucent, juicy pulp with a milder, more floral sweetness than its darker cousin. Grow in full sun to light shade on moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and expect a slow-growing tree that needs several years of steady watering before its first cauliflorous flush of white flowers and fruit. Harvest by hand as fruit colors fully and softens slightly, since jaboticaba of all kinds ferments and spoils quickly once picked.
sources: Morton, J. Fruits of Warm Climates

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs after last frost in full sun on well-drained soil; this naturally occurring hybrid between ketembilla and its African relative arose and was first propagated in Florida in 1953, running hardier and more productive than either parent species alone.

directions: Tropical apricot, sometimes called ketcot, is a hybrid of the ketembilla (Dovyalis hebecarpa) and its African relative Dovyalis abyssinica, grown for fruit that is juicier and more apricot-like in flavor than either parent, with the thin, fuzzy skin and deep red color of ketembilla. The spiny, dense shrub is more cold-tolerant and more productive than straight ketembilla, bearing over an extended season rather than one hard flush. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil, and plant more than one seedling or a grafted selection where possible, since fruit set improves with cross-pollination. Harvest when fruit has colored deeply and softens slightly, and expect a sharply acidic, apricot-tart flavor that mellows with a touch of sugar in jams, juice, or fresh eating once fully ripe.
sources: Growables.org — Tropical Apricot, Dovyalis hebecarpa x D. abyssinica
